title: Prompting & Structured Outputs
summary: A language model produces text. Your program needs data. This module is about closing that gap reliably, not with a nicer-sounding prompt, but with validation and repair logic that doesn't trust the model to behave.
objectives: Explain why raw model output is not a data format, and where that assumption breaks production systems
Design a prompt with a clear role, instructions, and few-shot examples that reduce output variance
Detect and repair the most common malformed-output patterns (code fences, trailing commas, extra prose)
Implement a real validator that checks output against a schema before your program trusts it

lessons.title: The gap between "sounds right" and "is data"
Few-shot examples reduce variance, not risk to zero
Before the checkpoint: what you should now be able to do

exercise.label: Code exercise · Python, runs in a real sandboxed Python interpreter (Pyodide)
exercise.instructions: Complete `extract_structured_output(raw_text, schema)`. `schema` is a dict `{"required": [...]}`, the list of field names that must be present. Return `{"ok": True, "data": ...}` on success, or `{"ok": False, "error": ...}` on failure, where `error` is a short human-readable string. Handle: markdown code fences around the JSON, a trailing comma before `}` or `]`, and a missing required field. Never raise, always return one of the two shapes above, even for completely non-JSON input.
exercise.starter:
import json
import re

def extract_structured_output(raw_text, schema):
    # Handle: markdown code fences, a trailing comma, and a missing required field.
    # Return {"ok": True, "data": ...} or {"ok": False, "error": ...}. Never raise.

    # YOUR CODE HERE

    pass

hints.title: Hint 1: conceptual
hints.mdx: Think in three passes: (1) clean up formatting noise around the JSON, (2) try to parse it, (3) check the parsed dict actually has what you need. Each pass can fail independently, and each failure should produce a useful error, not a raised exception.

hints.title: Hint 2: specific
hints.mdx: Python's `re` module: ````re.match(r"^```(?:json)?\s*([\s\S]*?)\s*```$", text)```` captures the content between fences. For trailing commas, `re.sub(r",\s*([}\]])", r"\1", text)` before parsing. Wrap `json.loads` in try/except, don't let it raise out of your function.

hints.title: Hint 3: near-solution
hints.mdx: After a successful parse, loop over `schema.get("required", [])` and check `field in data` for each one. Return a specific error naming the missing field on the first one that's absent, don't just say "invalid".

tests.name: Clean JSON parses correctly
tests.hint: A well-formed JSON string matching the schema should return {"ok": True, "data": ...} with the parsed values intact.

tests.name: Markdown code fence is stripped before parsing
tests.hint: Strip a leading/trailing ``` (optionally ```json) fence before attempting json.loads.

tests.name: Trailing comma is repaired before parsing
tests.hint: Replace a comma immediately before a closing } or ] with nothing before parsing.

tests.name: Missing required field is rejected with a specific error
tests.hint: After parsing, check every field in schema["required"] is present, and name the missing one in the error.

tests.name: Non-JSON prose is rejected gracefully, not raised
tests.hint: Wrap json.loads in try/except, plain prose will raise json.JSONDecodeError, catch it and return {"ok": False, "error": ...}.

questions.question: A model is instructed "respond only with valid JSON, no other text" and given two examples. What should a production system still do with its response?

options.text: Validate and parse it before trusting it, exactly as if it came from any other untrusted external source
options.why: Treat model output like any other untrusted input, validate before use.

options.text: Trust it directly, the instruction plus examples make malformed output effectively impossible
options.why: Instructions and examples reduce the RATE of malformed output, they don't reduce it to zero, a production system still needs to validate.

options.text: Log a warning but proceed with whatever text came back
options.why: Logging a warning after already acting on unvalidated data doesn't prevent the corruption or crash that malformed data can cause, validation has to happen before use, not after.

questions.principle: Treat model output like any other untrusted input, validate before use.

questions.question: Where does a standing output-format instruction (e.g. "always respond in JSON") most reliably belong?

options.text: The system role, stated once, reinforced with an example
options.why: The system role is for standing instructions that apply across the whole conversation.

options.text: Anywhere in the user message, position doesn't matter
options.why: Position does matter in practice, instructions buried mid-message compete with the actual request for the model's attention, a standing instruction belongs in the system role.

options.text: It should be repeated in every assistant turn instead of stated once
options.why: A standing instruction doesn't need to be repeated every turn if it's placed in the system role, that's exactly what the system role is for, persistent instructions that apply for the whole conversation.

questions.principle: The system role is for standing instructions that apply across the whole conversation.

questions.question: A response is `{"name": "Sam"}`, syntactically valid JSON, but your schema requires `age` too. Is this a repair-pass issue or a validation issue?

options.text: Validation, the JSON is syntactically fine, the repair pass has nothing to fix
options.why: Syntactically valid but semantically incomplete is a validation problem, not a repair-pass problem.

options.text: Repair pass, this is exactly what stripping trailing commas is for
options.why: There's no syntax problem here to repair, {"name": "Sam"} parses successfully, the issue is that the resulting DATA is incomplete, which is what validation checks for, not the repair pass.

options.text: Neither, this response should be accepted as-is
options.why: The response is missing a field your schema explicitly requires, accepting it as-is means your program later fails (or behaves wrong) when it tries to use the missing age field.

questions.principle: Syntactically valid but semantically incomplete is a validation problem, not a repair-pass problem.

questions.question: Why do few-shot examples typically improve output consistency more than a longer text description of the desired format?

options.text: A concrete example removes ambiguity a prose description leaves open (nesting, extra fields, exact key names)
options.why: Concrete examples remove interpretive ambiguity that prose descriptions leave open.

options.text: Examples make the prompt longer, and longer prompts are always more reliable
options.why: Length itself isn't what helps, a long, vague description doesn't outperform a short, concrete example. It's the removal of ambiguity that matters, not the character count.

options.text: Examples let the model skip following the system instructions entirely
options.why: Examples work alongside the system instructions, reinforcing them concretely, they don't replace or let the model ignore those instructions.

questions.principle: Concrete examples remove interpretive ambiguity that prose descriptions leave open.

questions.question: A response comes back as: ```` ```json\n{"status": "ok",}\n``` ````. After stripping the code fence and the trailing comma, is the remaining text valid JSON?

options.text: Yes, it becomes valid JSON
options.why: Correct. After stripping the fence and the trailing comma, the remaining text is {"status": "ok"}, which is valid JSON.

options.text: No, it's still invalid
options.why: Not quite. After stripping the ``` fence and the trailing comma before }, what's left is {"status": "ok"}, which IS valid JSON, that's exactly why the repair pass runs before parsing.

questions.question: A model returns ```json\n{"status": "ok",}\n``` (markdown fence, trailing comma). What is the correct order of operations before this data can be trusted?

options.text: Strip the markdown fence, remove the trailing comma, parse as JSON, then validate against the schema, in that order
Validate against the schema first, then repair whatever the validator flags
options.why: Schema validation needs a parsed object to inspect, you can't validate JSON you haven't successfully parsed yet, the fence and comma have to be fixed and the text parsed first.

options.text: Reject it immediately, a markdown fence means the model isn't following instructions
options.why: A markdown fence is one of the most common, easily-repaired deviations, rejecting outright throws away perfectly recoverable output instead of fixing it deterministically.

questions.question: Why must structured model output be validated even when the prompt explicitly asked for a specific JSON schema?
questions.objective: Explain why every model output needs validation

options.text: The model can still produce output that doesn't match the schema, asking for a shape doesn't guarantee the shape was produced
Validation is only needed if the prompt didn't specify a schema
options.why: A specified schema in the prompt is a strong hint to the model, not an enforced guarantee, the model can still deviate.

options.text: Validation is only needed for free-text responses, not JSON-shaped ones
options.why: JSON-shaped output is exactly what needs validation, malformed or incorrectly-typed JSON is a common failure mode this course covers directly.

questions.question: A repair function strips trailing commas AFTER attempting json.loads(). On input {"a": 1,} it raises instead of repairing. What's the bug?

options.text: The repair step runs after the parse attempt already failed, trailing-comma stripping has to happen BEFORE calling json.loads(), not after
json.loads() doesn't support trailing commas ever, so no repair order would fix this
options.why: json.loads() indeed rejects trailing commas, that's exactly why the repair step exists, to strip them before parsing, the bug is purely about step ORDER.

options.text: The regex used to strip commas is wrong
options.why: The described bug is about WHEN the repair runs relative to parsing, not the correctness of the stripping logic itself.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT something a deterministic repair pass can fix?
questions.objective: Distinguish a repairable defect from a non-repairable one

options.text: The model returning conversational prose instead of ever attempting JSON at all
A markdown code fence wrapped around otherwise-valid JSON
options.why: Stripping a fence is a simple, deterministic, always-safe repair, this is exactly the kind of thing a repair pass handles well.

options.text: A single trailing comma before a closing brace
options.why: Trailing commas are mechanically detectable and removable with a simple regex, a textbook repairable defect.

questions.question: After stripping fences and trailing commas, json.loads() still raises. What's the appropriate next step?
questions.objective: Know when to fall back to a model retry

options.text: Fall back to an expensive retry (re-prompting the model with the parse error included), since the cheap deterministic fixes didn't work
Give up and return the raw unparsed text to the caller as-is
options.why: Silently returning unusable text to a caller expecting structured data just moves the failure downstream instead of handling it.

options.text: Try stripping the trailing comma again, a second time
options.why: Repeating an already-attempted deterministic fix that didn't work won't produce a different result, the next step is escalating, not repeating.

questions.question: What planning-level relationship between characters and tokens does this course use?

options.text: tokens ≈ characters / 4
tokens ≈ characters × 4
options.why: This inverts the relationship, a token is roughly 4 characters, not 4 tokens per character.

options.text: tokens = words exactly, one token per word
options.why: Tokens are sub-word units, not whole words, punctuation and rare words often cost MORE than one token each.

questions.question: A required field is missing from an otherwise well-formed model response. What should the system do?
questions.objective: Decide how to surface a validation failure

options.text: Reject the response and surface a clear, structured error naming the missing field, rather than proceeding with incomplete data
Fill the missing field with a reasonable-looking default and continue silently
options.why: Silently fabricating a value for a required field hides a real problem and can produce confidently wrong downstream behavior.

options.text: Ignore the missing field if the rest of the response looks fine
options.why: A required field being missing is exactly the kind of defect validation exists to catch, ignoring it defeats the purpose of validating at all.

questions.question: A model asked for JSON responds: "Sure! Here's what I found: the user is 29." Why doesn't a repair pass fix this the way it fixes a trailing comma?
questions.objective: Recognize why prose isn't a parse failure to repair

options.text: There's no JSON structure present at all to repair, the model never attempted the format, repair only fixes small deviations from an otherwise-present structure
Because the response is too long for a repair pass to process
options.why: Length isn't the issue, structure is, a repair pass targets small syntactic deviations, not a complete absence of the requested format.

options.text: Because repair passes only work on responses under 100 characters
options.why: There's no length threshold involved, the issue is that prose has no JSON structure to repair in the first place.

questions.question: An insurance-claim intake bot asks a model to extract {"claimant_name": str, "incident_date": str, "amount": number} from a submitted description. It returns valid JSON, but amount is the string "about $2,400" instead of a number. Is this a repair-pass fix or a validation failure?
questions.objective: Apply repair-then-validate to a real intake form

options.text: A validation failure, the JSON parsed fine, the defect is a type mismatch (string where a number was required), that's schema validation's job to catch, not the repair pass's
A repair-pass fix, since "about $2,400" can be turned into 2400 with a bit of string cleanup
options.why: Even though a human could guess the intended number, this isn't a small syntactic defect like a trailing comma, silently coercing a fuzzy string into a number risks fabricating precision the source text didn't actually contain, that's a rejection-and-clarify case, not a mechanical repair.

options.text: Neither, since the JSON is syntactically valid the whole response should be accepted as-is
options.why: Syntactic validity (it parsed) and semantic correctness (the fields have the right types and meaning) are different checks, this response passes the first and fails the second.

questions.question: A structured-output validator's repair pass is triggered on 40% of calls to a particular prompt, and about half of those still fail validation even after repair. What does this pattern suggest about the fix?
questions.objective: Decide when repeated malformed output stops being a repair problem

options.text: The prompt itself likely needs to change, a repair pass masking a persistently bad hit rate is treating a systemic prompt problem as if it were an occasional parsing inconvenience
Nothing, a 40% repair rate is normal and expected for any structured-output prompt
options.why: A recurring, high repair-then-still-fails rate is a signal worth investigating, not a baseline to accept silently, it points at the prompt (or schema clarity) as the actual problem.

options.text: The repair pass needs more regex rules added until the failure rate reaches zero
options.why: Continuously patching repair logic to paper over a persistently bad hit rate treats a symptom, the more durable fix is improving the prompt or schema that's producing malformed output this often in the first place.

questions.question: A response fails to parse as JSON at all. Does it make sense to run schema validation against it anyway, "just in case"?
questions.objective: Distinguish parsing from validation as two separate stages

options.text: No, schema validation checks fields on a parsed object, if there's no parsed object yet there's nothing for the validator to inspect
Yes, validation can check the raw text directly without a successful parse first
options.why: Schema validation operates on structured data (an object with fields), not on raw unparsed text, a parse has to succeed first.

options.text: Yes, but only for schemas with fewer than five fields
options.why: Field count has no bearing on whether validation needs a successfully parsed object first, that requirement is unconditional.

glossary.definition: model output constrained to a predictable, parseable shape, typically JSON.
including example input/output pairs in the prompt to demonstrate the desired response shape.
the three message roles most model APIs use to separate standing instructions, the current request, and prior responses.
deterministic cleanup (stripping fences, trailing commas) attempted before treating a response as unparseable.
checking that successfully-parsed data actually contains the fields a consumer requires.

project.title: Structured Output Validator
project.brief: Build a tool that validates and repairs raw model output against a JSON schema: strips markdown fences, fixes trailing commas, reports what it couldn't fix.
